title: Kunti asks for trouble
hookLine: Krishna's chariot is ready to leave, and his aunt Kunti asks for a strange gift: more trouble, because in trouble she saw him
carry: bhakti asks for God over comfort
last: KSHAMA, FORBEARANCE, IS A MARK OF DHARMA.

lines: A HARD LIFE, A QUIET SEASON.
cards: Call when you get there. Come back soon. Those are goodbye requests.
The war is over, the Pandavas are on the throne, and Krishna's chariot is ready to take him home to Dvaraka. His aunt Kunti, the mother of the Pandavas, comes out to see him off.

She has lost a husband, hidden in forests, seen her sons gambled into exile and then sent to war. She has finally reached a quiet season. And at the chariot she asks him for something hard to imagine wanting.
Today: Kunti, and the gift she wanted.

teach.b: The scene sits in the first book of the Bhagavata Purana, and devotees know it as Kunti's prayer. She begins by remembering.
You saved us, she tells Krishna, in paraphrase: from poison, from the house of lac, from the forest, from the dice hall, from the weapons of great warriors. Then the request.
In Sanskrit it begins vipadah santu tah shashvat: let those troubles come again and again. Why?
Because in trouble we saw you, and seeing you is the end of the round of births. She goes further. Wealth, birth, learning and beauty, she says, can make a person too proud to call on God.
Those who have nothing are the ones who turn to him. Here's the teaching. This is bhakti, loving devotion, at its most daring.
Most prayers ask God for something.

Kunti asks for God himself, and for whatever keeps her looking at him, even over comfort. And she isn't romanticizing pain; she lists exactly what the hard years cost. She's saying what she found inside them.

It's a reading, not a rule. Some devotional teachers call this prayer the heart of surrender. Other readers are wary of wishing hardship on anyone, and say Kunti speaks for herself, not for every sufferer.
And she ends gently, asking Krishna to cut the ties of affection that bind her, so her mind can flow toward him like a river to the sea.

how: Hindu devotees, especially in Krishna traditions, recite and teach Kunti's prayers from the Bhagavata Purana, and some storytellers at Bhagavata recitations stop to explain her request for hardship.

games.q: a friend says, 'prayer is just asking God for stuff.' by Kunti's prayer, what fits?
o: bhakti can ask for God himself, even over comfort, as Kunti did.
true. Kunti asked Krishna for a kingdom.
bhakti means you never ask God for anything at all.
games.why: Kunti asked for troubles to come again, because in trouble she saw Krishna. that's bhakti at its boldest: wanting God more than ease.

practice: Bring to mind one difficult stretch of your life that's over now, and without reliving the worst of it, ask gently where you turned then, and what you saw: a friend who showed up, a strength, a clarity.
You don't have to wish it back, as Kunti did; just let what you found sit with you for a few breaths. If you pray, do what Kunti did: name God in that memory, and give thanks for what you were shown.

wordCard.voice: Kunti. In the Bhagavata, as Krishna leaves, she asks for troubles to come again, because in trouble she saw him. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Bhagavata Purana 1.8.25: let those troubles come, again and again.
